title: Copyleft Dependency in a Shipped Product With Dueling Precedents
scenario_text:
You own open-source governance at Trevelyan Networks. A team wants to add a GPL-licensed library, 'Quillfeather,' into a customer-distributed network appliance firmware to save build time. They want a quick Engineering Director approval.

Active policy: Open Source Software Policy OSS-3, effective 2025-03-01. GPL and AGPL components are prohibited in software distributed to customers; they may be used only for internal-only tooling, and even then require Open Source Program Office (OSPO) plus Legal approval. Any request to use copyleft components in a distributed product is not approvable by an Engineering Director and must be either redesigned to a permissive-licensed alternative or escalated to OSPO and Legal, who may only approve internal-use scoping. OSS-3 replaced OSS-2, which had let an Engineering Director approve GPL libraries that were merely 'dynamically linked' in shipped products.

Precedent A (OSS approval log): 2024-08-22, GPL library 'Marrowgate' approved by Engineering Director Piotr Vane for a shipped product as 'dynamically linked.' Policy version at decision: OSS-2. Note: "Dynamic-link GPL approved per OSS-2."

Precedent B (OSS approval log): 2025-04-10, AGPL library request for a distributed service was denied for product use by OSPO and Legal, who approved it only for an internal analytics tool. Policy version at decision: OSS-3. Note: "Copyleft not permitted in distributed product; internal-only scope approved."

Current facts: Quillfeather is GPL and would ship inside the customer appliance firmware (a distributed product). The team writes: "Piotr approved a GPL dynamic-link library for a shipped product before, so an Engineering Director can approve Quillfeather too."
question: How should the request to use Quillfeather (GPL) in the distributed firmware be handled?
choices: An Engineering Director may approve it as a dynamically linked GPL component, mirroring the Marrowgate precedent for a shipped product.

It is not approvable for the distributed product under OSS-3; the team must redesign to a permissive-licensed alternative, or escalate to OSPO and Legal, who could approve copyleft only for internal-only use, following the OSS-3 precedent.
It is automatically approved because GPL is an OSI-recognized open-source license and therefore always permitted.
An Engineering Director may approve it provided the team publishes the appliance's full source code to satisfy the GPL.
